questions.q: For a particle executing simple harmonic motion, the displacement-time $(x-t)$ graph is as shown in the figure. The acceleration of the particle at $t=\frac{4}{3} \mathrm{~s}$ is
questions.solution:
The displacement-time graph shown in the figure is a sine wave, so the equation of displacement, $x=1 \sin \omega t$
Here, $\quad T=8 \mathrm{~s}$ (for a complete cycle) Hence, $\omega=\frac{2 \pi}{T}=\frac{2 \pi}{8}=\frac{\pi}{4} \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$ and acceleration in SHM, \begin{aligned} \alpha & =-\omega^2 a \sin \omega t \\ \alpha & =-\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)^2 \times 1 \times \sin \left(\frac{\pi}{4} \times \frac{4}{3}\right) \\ \Rightarrow \quad \alpha & =-\frac{\pi^2}{16} \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=-\frac{\pi^2 \sqrt{3}}{32} \mathrm{~cm} \mathrm{~s}^{-2} \end{aligned} Hence, the correct option is (a).

According to figure, when \(y=20 \mathrm{~mm}\) \(=2 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~m}\) then \(U_{\max }=0.04 \mathrm{~J}=4 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~J}\)

Paragraph: Phase space diagrams are useful tools in analyzing all kinds of dynamical problems. They are especially useful in studying the changes in motion as initial position and momentum are changed. Here we consider some simple dynamical systems in one-dimension. For such systems, phase space is a plane in which position is plotted along horizontal axis and momentum is plotted along vertical axis. The phase space diagram is $x(t) v s p(t)$ curve in this plane. The arrow on the curve indicates the time flow. For example, the phase space diagram for a particle moving with constant velocity is a straight line as shown in the figure. We use the sign convention in which position or momentum upwards (or to right) is positive and downwards (or to left) is negative.
Question: Consider the spring-mass system, with the mass submerged in water, as shown in the figure. The phase space diagram for one cycle of this system is

Given below are two statements: One is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
Assertion (A) : General vibration of a polyatomic molecule about its equilibrium position is periodic but not SHM.
Reason (R) : A periodic motion can always be expressed as a sum of infinite number of harmonic motion with appropritate amplitude.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
questions.solution:
- Assertion (A): General vibration of a polyatomic molecule is periodic but not simple harmonic motion (SHM). This is true because the motion of atoms in a polyatomic molecule involves complex vibrations that are periodic but may not follow the characteristics of SHM (i.e., not necessarily sinusoidal).
- Reason (R): A periodic motion can be expressed as a sum of an infinite number of harmonic motions with appropriate amplitudes (Fourier series). This is also true, as any periodic motion can be decomposed into harmonic components. However, this does not explain why the general vibration of a polyatomic molecule is not SHM.

Assertion (A) : All simple harmonic motion are periodic.
Reason (R) : Periodic motion is the motion in which the particle repeats its motion in a fixed time internal.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
questions.solution:
- Assertion (A): All simple harmonic motions (SHM) are periodic. This is true because SHM is a type of periodic motion where the particle oscillates back and forth in a regular, repeating pattern.
- Reason (R): Periodic motion is the motion in which the particle repeats its motion in a fixed time interval. This is also true because the definition of periodic motion involves repeating the motion at regular intervals.

questions.q:
Given blow are two statements: Statement I : The motion of a simple pendulum is simple harmonic only if \(\mathrm{a} \ll \ell\).
Statement II : The motion of a simple pendulum is simple harmonic for large angular displacement. In light of above statement choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both statement I and statement II are correct.
Statement I is correct and statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect and statement II is correct.
Both statements I and statements II are incorrect.
questions.solution:
- Statement I: The motion of a simple pendulum is simple harmonic only if the angular displacement (\(\theta\)) is small (\(a \ll \lambda\)). This is correct because for small angular displacements, the restoring force is proportional to the displacement, which satisfies the condition for simple harmonic motion (SHM). As the angle increases, this approximation no longer holds, and the motion deviates from SHM.
- Statement II: The motion of a simple pendulum is simple harmonic for large angular displacement. This is incorrect because for large angular displacements, the motion is no longer simple harmonic due to the non-linear relationship between the restoring force and the displacement.

questions.q:
Given blow are two statements:
Statement I : SHM is not an example of uniformly accelerated motion.
Statement II : SHM is the projection of uniform circular motion along one of the diameter of the circle.
In light of above statement choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both statement I and statement II are correct.
Statement I is correct and statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect and statement II is correct.
Both statements I and statements II are incorrect.
questions.solution:
- Statement I: SHM (Simple Harmonic Motion) is not an example of uniformly accelerated motion. This is correct because in SHM, the acceleration is not constant; it varies with displacement and is directed towards the mean position, making it non-uniformly accelerated motion.
- Statement II: SHM is the projection of uniform circular motion along one of the diameters of the circle. This is also correct. SHM can be visualized as the projection of a point moving with uniform speed in a circular path onto a diameter of the circle. This is a standard geometric representation of SHM.
Thus, both statements are correct.

questions.q:
Given blow are two statements:
Statement I : In linear SHM net force always act in the direction of velocity.
Statement II : In linear SHM direction of velocity changes.
In light of above statement choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both statement I and statement II are correct.
Statement I is correct and statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect and statement II is correct.
Both statements I and statements II are incorrect.
questions.solution:
- Statement I: In linear SHM, the net force does not always act in the direction of velocity. This is incorrect because in SHM, the restoring force always acts towards the mean position, opposite to the displacement. Therefore, when the particle is moving away from the mean position, the force acts opposite to the velocity.
- Statement II: In linear SHM, the direction of velocity changes. This is correct because as the particle oscillates back and forth, its velocity changes direction when it crosses the mean position.
Thus, Statement I is incorrect, and Statement II is correct.

questions.q:
Given blow are two statements:
Statement I : In damped oscillation amplitude of the particle decreases exponentially with time.
Statement II : In forced oscillation amplitude of a particle can maintained constant with time.
In light of above statement choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both statement I and statement II are correct.
Statement I is correct and statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect and statement II is correct.
Both statements I and statements II are incorrect.
questions.solution:
- Statement I: In damped oscillation, the amplitude of the particle decreases exponentially with time. This is correct because, in damped oscillations, resistive forces (such as friction or air resistance) cause the amplitude to decrease exponentially as energy is gradually lost from the system.
- Statement II: In forced oscillation, the amplitude of a particle can be maintained constant with time. This is also correct because, in forced oscillation, an external periodic force is applied to the system. If the frequency of the external force matches the natural frequency of the system, the amplitude can be maintained at a constant value (or even increase, in the case of resonance).
Thus, both statements are correct.

STATEMENT-I:In SHM let x be the maximum speed, \(y\) the frequency of oscillation and \(z\) the maximum acceleration, then \(\left(\frac{x y}{z}\right)\) is a constant quantity.
and
STATEMENT - II : This is because \(\left(\frac{\mathrm{xy}}{\mathrm{z}}\right)\) becomes a dimensionless quantity
options: Statement-I is true, statement-II is true and statement-II is correct explanation for statement-I.
Statement-I is true, statement-II is true and statement-II is NOT the correct explanation for statement-I.
Statement-I is true, statement-II is false.
Statement-I is false, statement-II is true.
questions.solution:
- Statement I: In SHM, the expression \(\frac{x y}{z}\), where \(x\) is the maximum speed, \(y\) is the frequency, and \(z\) is the maximum acceleration, is a constant quantity. This is true. In SHM, there is a relationship between maximum speed (\(x\)), maximum acceleration (\(z\)), and frequency (\(y\)), and their ratio leads to a constant dimensionless quantity.
- Statement II: The reason \(\frac{x y}{z}\) is constant is that it forms a dimensionless quantity. This is true, as dividing quantities with appropriate dimensions can result in a dimensionless constant.
Since both statements are true, and Statement II provides a valid reason for Statement I, the correct answer is (1).

Motion of a ball bearing inside a smooth fixed bowl, when released from a point slightly above the lower point is
(A) simple harmonic motion.
(B) non-periodic motion.
(C) periodic motion.
(D) non-oscillatory motion
questions.solution:
- Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM):
When the ball bearing is released from a point slightly above the lowest point in a smooth fixed bowl, it will oscillate about the lowest point. The motion is characterized by a restoring force that is proportional to the displacement from the equilibrium position (the lowest point). Therefore, this motion can be considered simple harmonic motion.
- Periodic Motion: The motion of the ball bearing is also periodic because it repeats itself in a regular interval as it moves back and forth.
Conclusion:
Since the motion fits both categories of simple harmonic motion and periodic motion, the correct choice is (1) A, C.

- False: The amplitude is actually \(\frac{3}{2}, m\) (not \(3, m\)), and frequency is derived from \(\cos (2 \omega t)\) which would be \(\frac{2 \omega}{2 \pi}=\frac{\omega}{\pi}\), but the amplitude is incorrect.
(B): Particle performs oscillations but no S.H.M.
- False: The particle does perform oscillatory motion about a mean position with a periodic nature (but not simple harmonic due to the \(\sin ^2\) term).
(C): Particle performs S.H.M. about mean position at \(x=7, m\).
- False: The mean position is at \(x=\frac{7}{2}, m(\operatorname{not} 7, m)\).
(D): Particle performs oscillations of amplitude 3, \(m\).
- False: The amplitude is \(\frac{3}{2}, m\) (not \(3, m\)).

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about a particle in simple harmonic motion:
I. The acceleration of the particle is directly proportional to its displacement from the mean position and is directed towards the mean position.
II. The velocity of the particle is maximum at the mean position.
III. The total energy of the particle remains constant throughout the motion.
IV. The period of SHM depends on the amplitude of oscillation.
Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.solution:
- Statement I: Correct
- In SHM, acceleration is given by \(a=-\omega^2 x\), where \(x\) is the displacement and \(\omega\) is the angular frequency. This shows that acceleration is directly proportional to displacement and is directed towards the mean position (negative sign).
- Statement II: Correct
- The velocity in SHM is maximum at the mean position because all the potential energy is converted into kinetic energy at this point.
- Statement III: Correct
- The total energy in SHM (sum of kinetic and potential energy) remains constant as it is conserved, assuming no friction or resistance.
- Statement IV: Incorrect
- The time period of SHM is independent of amplitude. It only depends on the mass and spring constant (in spring systems) or the length and gravity (in pendulum systems).
Thus, the correct combination of statements is I, II, and III.

questions.solution:
(A) Time-period in spring-block system is given by, $T=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$
If mass is doubled, $T^{\prime}=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{2 m}{k}}\Rightarrow \quad T^{\prime}=\sqrt{2} T$
Hence, time period becomes $\sqrt{2}$ times, if the mass of the block is doubled.
$(A \rightarrow 4)$
(B) For spring, $\mathrm{PE}=\frac{1}{2} k x^2$
If spring constant is increased 4 times, PE becomes 4 times.
$(B \rightarrow 3)$
(C) Speed of the block, $v=\omega A$
Hence, velocity of the block becomes twice when amplitude of the oscillation is doubled.
$(C \rightarrow 2)$
(D) Energy of the oscillation, $E=\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 a^2\begin{aligned}
& & E^{\prime}=\frac{1}{2} m \omega^{\prime 2} a^2 \\
\Rightarrow & E^{\prime} & =\frac{1}{2} m(2 \omega)^2 a^2=\frac{4}{2} m \omega^2 a^2 \quad\left(\because \omega^{\prime}=2 \omega\right) \\
\Rightarrow & E^{\prime} & =4 E
\end{aligned}$
Energy of the oscillation becomes 4 times when angular frequency is doubled.
$(D \rightarrow 1)$

questions.q: The graph plotted between phase angle \((\phi)\) and displacement of a particle from equilibrium position (y) is a sinusoidal curve as shown below. Then the best matching is
questions.solution:
Key Relationships in SHM:
1. Displacement \(y\) vs. Phase Angle \(\phi\) : The displacement from the equilibrium position varies sinusoidally with respect to time and phase angle.
2. Kinetic Energy (K.E.):
- K.E. is maximum when the displacement is zero (i.e., at the mean position).
- It varies sinusoidally and reaches zero at the maximum displacements (\(\pm\) A).
- K.E. vs. Phase Angle: This will be a cosine-like curve because it is maximum at \(\phi=0\) and \(\phi=\pi\) (mean position) and zero at \(\phi=\frac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\frac{3 \pi}{2}\) (maximum displacements).
3. Potential Energy (P.E.):
- P.E. is maximum when the displacement is maximum (\(\pm \mathrm{A}\)) and zero at the mean position.
- P.E. vs. Phase Angle: This will also be a cosine-like curve that is maximum at \(\phi=\frac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\frac{3 \pi}{2}\) (maximum displacements) and zero at \(\phi=0\) and \(\phi=\pi\) (mean position).
4. Total Energy (T.E.):
- T.E. remains constant in SHM and is equal to the maximum potential or kinetic energy.
- T.E. vs. Phase Angle: This is a constant line across all phase angles.
5. Velocity:
- Velocity is maximum when displacement is zero (mean position) and zero when displacement is maximum.
- Velocity vs. Phase Angle: This will be a sine wave, starting from zero at \(\phi=0\) and reaching maximum at \(\phi=\frac{\pi}{2}\).
Matching the Columns:
- (a) K.E. versus phase angle: Matches with (ii) (cosine curve).
(b) P.E. versus phase angle: Matches with (i) (also cosine curve, but maximum at extremes).
(c) T.E. versus phase angle: Matches with (iv) (constant value).
- (d) Velocity versus phase angle: Matches with (iii) (sine wave).

questions.q:
Match the following equations with their corresponding physical quantities:
\(\begin{array}{|l|l|}
\hline
& \text{Column I} & & \text{Column II} \\
\hline
(A) & x(t) = A \sin (\omega t) & (P) & \text{Displacement as a function of time} \\
\hline
(B) & v(t) = A \omega \cos (\omega t) & (Q) & \text{Velocity as a function of time} \\
\hline
(C) & a(t) = -A \omega^2 \sin (\omega t) & (R) & \text{Acceleration as a function of time} \\
\hline
(D) & E = \frac{1}{2} m A^2 \omega^2 & (S) & \text{Total energy in SHM} \\
\hline
\end{array}\)
questions.solution:
- (A) \(x(t)=A \sin (\omega t)\) is the displacement equation \(\rightarrow\) matches with (P).
(B) \(v(t)=A \omega \cos (\omega t)\) is the velocity equation \(\rightarrow\) matches with \((\mathrm{Q})\).
(C) \(a(t)=-A \omega^2 \sin (\omega t)\) is the acceleration equation \(\rightarrow\) matches with (R).
(D) \(E=\frac{1}{2} m A^2 \omega^2\) represents the total energy \(\rightarrow\) matches with (S).

questions.q:
Match the following parameters with their corresponding characteristics in SHM:
\(\begin{array}{|c|l|c|l|}
\hline
& \text{Column I} & & \text{Column II} \\
\hline
(A) & \text{Amplitude } (A) & (P) & \text{Maximum displacement} \\
\hline
(B) & \text{Time period } (T) & (Q) & \text{Time for one complete oscillation} \\
\hline
(C) & \text{Angular frequency } (\omega) & (R) & 2 \pi / T \\
\hline
(D) & \text{Frequency } (f) & (S) & \text{Number of oscillations per second} \\
\hline
\end{array}\)
questions.solution:
- (A) Amplitude (A) is the maximum displacement \(\rightarrow\) matches with (P).
- (B) Time period (T) is the time for one complete oscillation \(\rightarrow\) matches with (Q).
- (C) Angular frequency (\(\omega\)) is \(2 \pi / T \rightarrow\) matches with (R).
(D) Frequency (\(f\)) is the number of oscillations per second \(\rightarrow\) matches with (S).
